This produces family counts of 13 biological, five synthesis, six materials and two physical/theoretical awards: historical shares of 50%, 19%, 23% and 8%, respectively. The record supports a broad interpretation of Chemistry. It does not support a rule that a field is “due,” or that adjacent subjects cannot win close together ([official motivations](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/lists/all-nobel-prizes-in-chemistry/all/?gallery_style=page)).

I investigated four questions that could change the estimate: whether sequencing had a genuinely fresh recognition signal; whether Other contained concrete competitors; whether recent validation changed younger technologies’ readiness; and whether recognition of a scientist actually concerned the listed discovery.

**Sequencing has the strongest listed recognition pipeline.** The same trio received the 2022 Breakthrough Prize, announced on September 9, 2021, and the 2024 Gairdner recognition ([Breakthrough announcement](https://breakthroughprize.org/News/65), [Gairdner announcement](https://www.gairdner.org/resource-hub/2024-canada-gairdner-award-winners-announced)). They then received the Asturias award on May 13, 2026, and Zurich’s Chemistry prize, announced on August 27, 2026 ([Asturias jury](https://www.fpa.es/en/princess-of-asturias-awards/laureates/2026-david-klenerman-shankar-balasubramanian-pascal-mayer/?texto=acta), [University of Zurich](https://news.uzh.ch/de/articles/news/2026/gretener-thuerlemann-preis.html)). The new Wolf Chemistry award recognizes the same discovery package. Its account explicitly connects surface DNA-colony amplification with Solexa’s sequencing-by-synthesis chemistry ([Wolf Foundation](https://wolffund.org.il/pascal-mayer/)). This is stronger than generic praise for genomics. I give the combined recognition a substantial uplift, but do not count each award as independent evidence of Nobel intent.

**Other contains serious competitors, not just surprises.** Clarivate’s September 17, 2026 Chemistry selections cover three unlisted discovery clusters: self-assembled monolayers, long-range protein electron transfer, and base/prime editing. Clarivate explicitly says its program does not predict recipients in a particular year ([Clarivate announcement](https://clarivate.com/news/clarivate-reveals-citation-laureates-2026-recognizing-transformative-scientific-breakthroughs/)). The omissions have support beyond that list. Monolayers received the 2022 Kavli Nanoscience Prize; Liu’s editing technologies received the 2025 Breakthrough recognition; and modern systems proteomics received the 2026 Gairdner award ([Kavli](https://www.kavliprize.org/prizes/nanoscience/2022), [Harvard](https://www.chemistry.harvard.edu/news/2025/04/david-liu-receives-breakthrough-prize-life-sciences), [Gairdner](https://www.gairdner.org/resource-hub/2026-canada-gairdner-award-winners)). Buchwald–Hartwig amination and biomolecular condensates add distinct omitted contenders ([Wolf citation](https://wolffund.org.il/category/field/page/7/), [Clarivate’s earlier selections](https://clarivate.com/news/clarivate-unveils-citation-laureates-2025/)).

Recent validation strengthens several listed alternatives, but not enough to make them favorites. FDA approved the heterobifunctional protein degrader vepdegestrant on May 1, 2026. That removes the argument that targeted degradation lacks an approved therapeutic application; it does not establish decades of broad clinical impact ([FDA](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/resources-information-approved-drugs/fda-approves-vepdegestrant-er-positive-her2-negative-esr1-mutated-advanced-or-metastatic-breast)). Perovskites received fresh Kyoto recognition, while the award’s own explanation still identifies operational lifespan and environmental challenges ([Kyoto announcement](https://www.kyotoprize.org/260619-j), [scientific citation](https://www.kyotoprize.org/en/laureates/tsutomu_miyasaka/)). Langer’s May 19, 2026 Welch Chemistry award explicitly supports engineered-material delivery of therapeutic macromolecules, strengthening delivery’s Chemistry case rather than merely its biomedical importance ([Welch Foundation](https://welch1.org/news-reports/news/the-welch-foundation-announces-2026-welch-award-recipient)).

For the numerical construction, I combine a discovery-first allocation with a historical-family allocation. The following dimensionless weights are my judgments about this year’s readiness. They are not nomination counts, citation-derived probabilities or fitted likelihood ratios.

| Discovery | Weight | Main basis for the allocation |
|---|---:|---|
| Controlled radical polymerization | 7.0 | Mature, chemistry-central control of polymer construction, with established industrial utility ([Franklin Institute](https://fi.edu/en/awards/laureates/mitsuo-sawamoto)). |
| Sequencing-by-synthesis | 22.0 | Transformative platform and the strongest concentrated recognition signal ([Wolf](https://wolffund.org.il/pascal-mayer/)). |
| Solid-state perovskite cells | 5.0 | Strong discovery-specific awards; practical reliability remains a qualification ([NIMS](https://www.nims.go.jp/nims-award-symposium/2025/nims-award.html), [Kyoto](https://www.kyotoprize.org/en/laureates/tsutomu_miyasaka/)). |
| Phosphoramidite DNA synthesis | 5.3 | A discrete chemical invention underlying automated nucleic-acid synthesis ([Merkin award account](https://www.broadinstitute.org/news/inaugural-merkin-prize-biomedical-technology-awarded-dr-marvin-caruthers-developing-technology)). |
| C–H functionalization | 6.0 | Fundamental synthetic chemistry, supported by discovery-specific recognition ([Bergman’s Wolf citation](https://wolffund.org.il/category/field/page/8/)). |
| Polymeric/lipid delivery | 6.0 | Established impact and fresh Chemistry-specific recognition ([Welch](https://welch1.org/news-reports/news/the-welch-foundation-announces-2026-welch-award-recipient)). |
| Targeted protein degradation | 4.0 | Real therapeutic validation, but recent relative to older platforms ([FDA](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/resources-information-approved-drugs/fda-approves-vepdegestrant-er-positive-her2-negative-esr1-mutated-advanced-or-metastatic-breast)). |
| Molecular chaperones | 4.2 | Mature foundational discovery; substantial competition for recognition in Medicine ([Lasker](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/chaperone-assisted-protein-folding/)). |
| Nanopore methods | 2.5 | Established single-molecule analysis and sequencing; less compelling timing evidence in the sources examined ([Oxford](https://www.chem.ox.ac.uk/people/professor-hagan-bayley)). |
| Ab initio molecular dynamics | 2.7 | Foundational computational methodology with established recognition ([Dreyfus](https://www.dreyfus.org/michele-parrinello-2017/)). |
| Efficient OLEDs | 5.3 | Strong efficiency advances; the fresh recognition is classified under Physics, not Chemistry ([Clarivate](https://clarivate.com/news/clarivate-reveals-citation-laureates-2026-recognizing-transformative-scientific-breakthroughs/)). |
| DNA origami | 1.5 | Distinct programmable assembly; a weaker comparative near-term case in my assessment ([foundational paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04586)). |
| Other | 37.0 | Several identifiable, independently recognized discoveries plus the remaining field ([Clarivate](https://clarivate.com/citation-laureates/chemistry/), [Gairdner](https://www.gairdner.org/resource-hub/2026-canada-gairdner-award-winners)). |

The discovery-first model, A, divides each weight by their total, 108.5. The family model, B, uses the historical fractions 13/26, 5/26, 6/26 and 2/26. Within each family, it distributes that fraction in proportion to the listed weights plus an omitted-discovery reserve. My reserves are 15 for biological chemistry, seven for synthesis, 12 for materials and five for physical/theoretical chemistry. Controlled polymerization and C–H chemistry enter synthesis; perovskites, OLEDs and origami enter materials; molecular dynamics enters physical/theoretical chemistry; the remaining named options enter biological chemistry. Other receives the sum of the omitted allocations.

The final calculation is:

$$
 p_i=0.75A_i+0.25B_i.
$$

Here, A is the discovery-first probability and B is the historical-family probability. The blend favors current discovery-specific evidence without letting an attractive candidate list crowd out omitted fields. All allocation and blending coefficients are subjective. The JSON preserves the calculated distribution to six decimal places and sums exactly to one.

## What's non-obvious

The Wolf announcement’s proximity to Nobel week makes it unusually salient, not unusually transparent. Reporting places the announcement on Thursday evening, October 1, before the client’s question ([contemporaneous reporting](https://www.ynet.co.il/environment-science/article/r1ozk1h9gg)). Under the Nobel’s published timetable, recommendations were due in September. The late Wolf announcement therefore supplies corroboration of scientific standing, not evidence that it caused, leaked or coordinated with the Nobel decision ([selection timetable](https://www.nobelprize.org/chemistry)). This distinction prevents a strong signal from becoming an unjustified near-certainty.

Discovery matching also changes the forecast. Hartwig winning for carbon–heteroatom coupling would not automatically count as C–H functionalization: his joint Wolf citation with Buchwald concerns the former discovery ([Wolf citation](https://wolffund.org.il/category/field/page/7/)). Conversely, recognition of different pioneers of high-efficiency OLEDs can still match the listed OLED discovery ([Clarivate’s OLED selection](https://clarivate.com/news/clarivate-reveals-citation-laureates-2026-recognizing-transformative-scientific-breakthroughs/)). I therefore separate discovery uncertainty from uncertainty about the laureate roster.

## Uncertainties

The largest missing evidence is the committee’s actual candidate ranking and intended motivation. Confidential nominations and evaluations prevent direct verification. I also lack a validated same-year conversion model for precursor awards; correlated prize recognition cannot substitute for one ([Nobel confidentiality rules](https://www.nobelprize.org/chemistry), [Clarivate’s methodological caveat](https://clarivate.com/news/clarivate-reveals-citation-laureates-2026-recognizing-transformative-scientific-breakthroughs/)). A broad or divided sequencing motivation could also require careful application of the client’s discovery and share rules.

The central estimate is sensitive to the omitted pool and the strength assigned to sequencing’s fresh awards. In calculation stress tests, I varied omitted weights and reserves by 25%, sequencing’s weight from 16.8 to 26.4, and the discovery-first blend from 60% to 90%. Sequencing ranged from 15% to 25%; Other ranged from 27% to 41.6%. These are model-sensitivity ranges, not calibrated confidence intervals. The stable conclusion is the ranking: sequencing leads the named discoveries, while Other remains the largest combined category. The decimal precision records the arithmetic, not equally precise knowledge of a secret decision.
sub_write_ups:
## Forecast summary

My highest-probability listed outcome is **massively parallel sequencing-by-synthesis of DNA**, principally because an already Nobel-caliber discovery received an unusually concentrated sequence of precursor awards, culminating in **two independent 2026 awards to the same three-person team**. Nevertheless, Nobel selection remains highly opaque, and several prominent 2026 candidates are not represented by the listed discoveries. I therefore retain **26.2% for Other**.

The official announcement is scheduled for **Wednesday, October 7, 2026, at 11:45 CEST at the earliest**. Nobel nominations and evaluations remain confidential for 50 years; the Chemistry Committee submitted its recommendations in September, and the full Academy will make the final selection in October.

## Interpretation

I interpret each option by the **scientific discovery**, not by requiring the named people to be the exact laureates, consistent with the resolution criteria. This matters for OLEDs, nanopore sequencing, controlled radical polymerization, and C–H functionalization, where several plausible laureate configurations exist. Public events before the question was submitted are relevant evidence because the target is the future October 7 announcement, rather than an event that could already have resolved the question.

## Method

I assessed each discovery on five dimensions:

1. **Transformative impact and maturity (30%)** — whether impact has been demonstrated for long enough to resemble past Nobel work.
2. **Attribution and motivation fit (20%)** — whether the Academy can formulate a concise official motivation and select no more than three living laureates without an especially conspicuous omission.
3. **Fit with recent Chemistry prizes (15%)** — a soft penalty, not a rule, for close repetition of themes awarded in 2020–2025.
4. **Major precursor awards (25%)** — especially awards recognizing the same discovery and approximately the same group of pioneers.
5. **Weak 2025–2026 signals (10%)** — commercialization, first regulatory validation, unusually timed prizes, specialist commentary, and other developments that may indicate that a field's impact has recently become undeniable.

I first reserved a probability for **Other**, then distributed the remaining probability among the twelve named discoveries. Conditional on a listed option winning, my distribution is approximately: sequencing-by-synthesis 34.15%, perovskites 12.33%, targeted protein degradation 9.62%, C–H functionalization 8.13%, molecular chaperones 6.78%, controlled radical polymerization 6.10%, phosphoramidite synthesis 5.56%, OLEDs 5.28%, nanopores 4.07%, ab initio molecular dynamics 3.39%, lipid/polymeric delivery 3.25%, and DNA origami 1.36%.

## Historical base rates and field rotation

The Chemistry Nobel was awarded **117 times through 2025**, to 200 laureate-awards representing 198 individuals. The recent sequence was genome editing in 2020, asymmetric organocatalysis in 2021, click/bioorthogonal chemistry in 2022, quantum dots in 2023, computational protein design and structure prediction in 2024, and metal–organic frameworks in 2025.

There is no mechanical rotation, but this history gives modest penalties to:

- another protein-structure/folding prize immediately after 2024;
- another semiconductor or materials prize after quantum dots in 2023 and MOFs in 2025;
- another computational-modeling prize after 2013 and 2024.

Conversely, a broadly enabling analytical technique or classical reaction/polymer methodology would be less repetitive. Modern science Nobels commonly arrive decades after the foundational work; recent analyses put the average lag near 30 years for Chemistry in the past decade. That favors discoveries dating from the 1980s through early 2000s and makes most listed choices mature enough.

## Option-by-option assessment

### 1. Massively parallel sequencing-by-synthesis — **25.2%**

This is the strongest weak-signal cluster. Balasubramanian, Klenerman, and Mayer received the **2026 Wolf Prize in Chemistry** for low-cost, large-scale DNA sequencing and the **2026 Princess of Asturias Award** for next-generation sequencing. The Wolf announcement became public on October 2, only five days before the Nobel announcement. Because the Nobel Committee submitted its report in September, the Wolf decision cannot causally influence that report; its value is as evidence that an independent elite scientific jury converged on the exact discovery and trio at almost the same time.

The same work had already received the Millennium Technology Prize in 2020, Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences in 2022, Canada Gairdner International Award in 2024, and Novo Nordisk Prize in 2024. The technology has transformed genomics, medicine, pathogen surveillance, and cancer research, while providing an unusually tidy three-person attribution.

Chemistry World's news editor independently selected this as his top 2026 tip, describing it as a perennial Nobel candidate whose impact and precursor prizes make it highly plausible.

The main negatives are that it might be considered more appropriate for Physiology or Medicine, and Chemistry has recently rewarded DNA repair, CRISPR, and protein-related work. Even with the unusually strong signal, secrecy and the annual multiplicity of Nobel-worthy discoveries keep it well below 50%.

### 2. Other — **26.2%**

The option list is strong but far from exhaustive. Current prominent omitted areas include self-assembled monolayers, biological electron transfer, base and prime editing, glycoscience, biomolecular condensates, single-atom catalysis, photocatalysis, optogenetics, RAS-targeted chemistry, Buchwald–Hartwig amination, and energy-storage chemistry.

Clarivate's 2026 additions included researchers working on self-assembled monolayers, gene-editing tools, biological electron transfer, and high-efficiency OLED approaches. Chemistry World's discussion specifically treated several omitted discoveries—Harry Gray's biological electron-transfer work, self-assembled monolayers, RAS-targeting chemistry, and other analytical techniques—as credible possibilities.

A low-liquidity prediction-market check was performed only after forming my independent estimate. A third-party Kalshi display put omitted candidates David Allara and Harry Gray at 18% and 17%, while Balasubramanian was at 7%. However, it reported only about **$2,800 in 24-hour volume**, a medium-quality score of 52/100, and separate single-person contracts rather than a mutually exclusive discovery-level distribution. I therefore treated it as evidence that **Other must remain substantial**, not as a reliable quantitative correction.

### 3. Solid-state perovskite solar cells — **9.1%**

The exact listed trio—Miyasaka, Snaith, and Park—received the **2025 NIMS Award** for developing and advancing practical perovskite solar cells. Miyasaka then received the **2026 Kyoto Prize** for creating perovskite photovoltaic technology.

The technology also crossed a meaningful maturity threshold: Oxford PV began commercial tandem-cell production in 2024, while a 2026 review reported laboratory efficiencies around 27% for single-junction devices and above 34.5% for perovskite–silicon tandems, alongside improving stability and industrial scalability. These are efficiency percentages, not probabilities, and refer to laboratory photovoltaic performance.

It is held below sequencing because the decisive solid-state breakthroughs date mainly to 2012, commercialization is only now beginning, and a 2026 award would follow materials prizes in 2023 and 2025.

### 4. Targeted protein degradation — **7.1%**

The crucial new signal is clinical validation. On **May 1, 2026**, the FDA approved vepdegestrant, a heterobifunctional protein degrader, following a randomized trial of 624 patients; specialist coverage characterized it as the first approved PROTAC and a major validation of the targeted-degradation modality.

Crews and Deshaies also received the 2025 Passano Award after earlier recognition for originating PROTACs.

This is exactly the sort of weak signal that can move a field from “promising platform” to “demonstrated benefit.” The negatives are its proximity to the 2004 ubiquitin-mediated degradation Nobel and the 2024 protein prize, plus unresolved attribution between PROTAC pioneers, molecular-glue work, and later clinical developers. One approval may still be too little for the Academy.

### 5. Transition-metal-catalyzed C–H functionalization — **6.0%**

This is arguably the best traditional-chemistry candidate. It is mature, conceptually fundamental, extensively used in synthesis, and lends itself to a Nobel-style motivation about converting normally inert C–H bonds directly into functionalized products.

Hartwig received the 2019 Wolf Prize and, with Avelino Corma and Helmut Schwarz, a **2025 BBVA Frontiers of Knowledge Award** for advances in catalysis. The award materials specifically cited Hartwig's work on C–H bond cleavage and applications in large-scale pharmaceutical chemistry.

Two independent historical-pattern reviews I commissioned ranked C–H functionalization first, emphasizing its mature impact and pure-Chemistry fit. I discounted it relative to those reviews because the field is very broad: Bergman, Murai, Hartwig, Yu, Sanford, White, and others have substantial claims, making a three-person choice unusually contentious. Chemistry World's discussion reached the same conclusion: it is repeatedly suggested, but selecting only three contributors is difficult.

### 6. Molecular chaperones — **5.0%**

Hartl and Horwich have accumulated an exceptionally strong collection of precursor awards. Most recently, Hartl received the **2026 Keio Medical Science Prize**, announced September 18, for establishing the paradigm of chaperone-assisted intracellular protein folding. Keio reports that thirteen previous recipients subsequently received Nobels, although this is not an annual hit rate and many awards crossed categories or involved long lags.

The discovery is mature and attribution to Hartl and Horwich is relatively clean. The large penalties are category fit—it may be more likely in Medicine—and close thematic proximity to the 2024 Chemistry Nobel for protein structure prediction and design.

### 7. Controlled radical polymerization — **4.5%**

Controlled radical polymerization is a highly mature and industrially important platform. Matyjaszewski and Sawamoto independently reported atom-transfer radical polymerization in 1995; their work received the 2017 Franklin Medal, while Matyjaszewski received the 2011 Wolf Prize and a 2023 National Academy of Sciences award.

The drawback is attribution. A broad prize should recognize ATRP, RAFT, and possibly nitroxide-mediated polymerization, but three slots cannot comfortably accommodate Matyjaszewski, Sawamoto, Rizzardo, Moad, Thang, and the NMP pioneers. The listed trio is plausible but not uniquely compelling.

### 8. Phosphoramidite chemistry for automated DNA synthesis — **4.1%**

This is one of the most foundational enabling technologies on the list. The Caruthers laboratory's early-1980s chemistry made efficient, iterative synthesis of DNA possible and helped create routine automated DNA synthesis. It underpins PCR primers, sequencing, synthetic biology, oligonucleotide drugs, gene construction, and much of biotechnology. Caruthers received the inaugural Merkin Prize in 2023 for this technology.

I used a hierarchical allocation so that twelve attractive named discoveries would not crowd out Other simply by being listed.

| Biological | Sequencing 0.285; phosphoramidite 0.110; delivery 0.140; degradation 0.140; chaperones 0.075; nanopore 0.045; Other 0.205 |
| Synthetic | Controlled radical polymerization 0.370; C–H functionalization 0.270; Other 0.360 |
| Materials/physical | OLED 0.310; perovskites 0.140; DNA origami 0.080; Other 0.470 |
| Computational/theoretical | Ab initio molecular dynamics 0.600; Other 0.400 |

These are **subjective forecasting inputs**, informed by the evidence above. They are not estimated nomination frequencies, citation-derived probabilities, or outputs from a validated regression.

Second, after the additional research, I multiplied the sequencing conditional weight by **1.5** for the newly verified Wolf recognition and the perovskite weight by **1.8** for the Kyoto evidence. These are conservative judgmental evidence multipliers, not empirically estimated likelihood ratios. I then renormalized within the affected fields, keeping total field probabilities fixed to avoid allowing one precursor award to overwhelm the historical baseline.

The biological normalization constant is:

`Z_bio = 1 + 0.285 × (1.5 − 1) = 1.1425`.

Therefore:

`P(sequencing) = 0.48 × 0.285 × 1.5 / 1.1425 = 0.1796061269…`.

The materials normalization constant is:

`Z_materials = 1 + 0.140 × (1.8 − 1) = 1.112`.

Therefore:

`P(perovskites) = 0.24 × 0.140 × 1.8 / 1.112 = 0.0543884892…`.

Other is the sum of the unlisted allocations across all four fields:

`P(Other) = 0.48 × 0.205 / 1.1425 + 0.22 × 0.360 + 0.24 × 0.470 / 1.112 + 0.06 × 0.400 = 0.2907657636…`.

Every remaining listed probability follows by multiplying its field probability by its conditional weight, divided by the applicable normalization constant. I performed this calculation in Python with decimal arithmetic. I converted the results to four decimal places using largest-remainder rounding, which preserves an exact total of **1.0000**.

([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/resources-information-approved-drugs/fda-approves-vepdegestrant-er-positive-her2-negative-esr1-mutated-advanced-or-metastatic-breast?utm_source=openai))

### D. Discovery-level matching changes the treatment of C–H chemistry

Bergman's **2017 Wolf Chemistry Prize** specifically recognized transition-metal activation of hydrocarbon C–H bonds, supporting the listed field. However, Clarivate's **2020 recognition of Hartwig and Buchwald** emphasized amination through coupling amines with aryl halides. That is not interchangeable with C–H functionalization. I retain substantial probability for the listed discovery while reserving separate Other probability for an amination/cross-coupling award. The reduction is about the discovery being rewarded—not a requirement that the option's three names match. ([wolffund.org.il](https://wolffund.org.il/page/123/?cs=807&dir=site&lang=&page=winners&utm_source=openai))

## 4. Assessment of the remaining listed discoveries

**Controlled radical polymerization:** this has a strong chemistry-native case: general control over polymer synthesis, extensive materials applications and mature independent recognition. CMU's **17 February 2011** announcement of Matyjaszewski's Wolf Prize expressly connected the award to controlled polymer synthesis and ATRP. It remains a serious candidate. I do not interpret its long wait as an increasing mechanical entitlement to win this year; nor do I view the several mechanisms under the umbrella as a perfectly simple attribution problem. ([cmu.edu](https://www.cmu.edu/news/stories/archives/2011/february/feb17_wolfprize.html?utm_source=openai))

**Phosphoramidite DNA synthesis:** the Broad Institute's **28 June 2023** Merkin Prize announcement documents the 1981 chemistry, the contributions of Beaucage and Matteucci, and its role in automated nucleic-acid synthesis. This provides a particularly clear distinction from sequencing: writing DNA rather than reading it. Its foundational character warrants approximately the same probability as controlled radical polymerization, but I found less compelling current-year timing evidence than for sequencing or delivery. ([broadinstitute.org](https://www.broadinstitute.org/news/inaugural-merkin-prize-biomedical-technology-awarded-dr-marvin-caruthers-developing-technology?utm_source=openai))

**Efficient OLEDs:** the September 2026 Citation Laureates recognized Thompson, Forrest and Adachi for high-efficiency OLED technologies—but under **Physics**. Different names would not prevent a Chemistry award from matching this option. The scientific recognition is positive, while possible recognition in Physics limits how strongly I transfer that signal to Chemistry. Hence only a modest multiplier. ([clarivate.com](https://clarivate.com/news/clarivate-reveals-citation-laureates-2026-recognizing-transformative-scientific-breakthroughs/?utm_source=openai))

**Molecular chaperones:** Hartl and Horwich received the **2011 Lasker Basic Award** for chaperone-assisted protein folding. This is strong evidence of a mature discovery. I retain meaningful Chemistry probability, with a modest discount for the possibility of recognition in Medicine and competition from other protein-related discoveries. The 2024 protein-design/prediction prize is adjacent, but not the same discovery. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/2011-winners/?utm_source=openai))

**Nanopore analysis and sequencing:** the inventors' **6 May 2016** historical account documents origins across several laboratories, the single-molecule sensing principle and commercialization. The approach is technically distinct from sequencing-by-synthesis and could merit its own prize. My lower probability reflects weaker timing evidence in this research and a more distributed development narrative. I do not use the 2016 review's performance figures as current 2026 measurements. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/6733523/?utm_source=openai))

**Ab initio molecular dynamics:** the Franklin Institute records the **1985 Car–Parrinello breakthrough** and their **2021 Chemistry medal**. This is an established, broadly useful computational method. I assign a small positive probability while discounting competition from other computational advances and proximity to prior recognition of quantum-chemical computation and multiscale modeling. Those earlier prizes do not make it ineligible. ([fi.edu](https://fi.edu/en/awards/laureates/roberto-car?utm_source=openai))

**DNA origami:** Rothemund's foundational paper was published on **16 March 2006** and provides a sharply identifiable programmable-assembly method. It is a genuine contender, not merely a speculative application. My lower assessment is a judgment about comparatively weaker timing evidence and demonstrated field-wide impact—not a claim that a Nobel requires mass-market commercialization. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04586?utm_source=openai))

## 5. Reproducible numerical construction

I used a normalized-weight elicitation model. The reference weights represent durable scientific importance, maturity, independent recognition and omitted-field breadth. They are **judgmental inputs, not observed nomination counts**. Multipliers incorporate current recognition, validation, discovery-boundary corrections and discipline competition.

| Discovery | Reference weight b | Evidence multiplier m | Updated weight b × m |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Controlled radical polymerization | 5 | 1.00 | 5 |
| Massively parallel sequencing-by-synthesis | 11 | 1.65 | 18.15 |
| Solid-state perovskite solar cells | 3 | 1.35 | 4.05 |
| Phosphoramidite DNA synthesis | 5 | 1.00 | 5 |
| C–H functionalization | 5 | 0.85 | 4.25 |
| Polymeric/lipid nanoparticle delivery | 6 | 1.30 | 7.8 |
| Targeted protein degradation | 1.5 | 1.55 | 2.325 |
| Molecular chaperones | 4 | 0.90 | 3.6 |
| Nanopore methods | 2 | 0.90 | 1.8 |
| Ab initio molecular dynamics | 2 | 0.85 | 1.7 |
| Efficient OLEDs | 3.5 | 1.15 | 4.025 |
| DNA origami | 1.5 | 0.90 | 1.35 |
| Other | 40 | 1.10 | 44 |
| **Total** | **89.5** | | **103.05** |

To avoid overreacting to publicity and correlated prize signals, I mix the updated distribution with the reference distribution:

**p(i) = 0.80 × [b(i)m(i) / 103.05] + 0.20 × [b(i) / 89.5].**

For example, sequencing's probability is **0.80 × 18.15/103.05 + 0.20 × 11/89.5 = 0.165483480114** before output rounding. Other's corresponding value is **0.430967231289**. I performed the normalization and sensitivity calculations in Python. The JSON reports nine decimal places, with Other adjusted by approximately two billionths so the reported values sum exactly to 1.000000000.

This construction makes the arithmetic reproducible. It does not make the elicited weights uniquely correct: another informed forecaster could reasonably choose different weights from the same evidence.

## 6. Sensitivity, data quality and limitations

The largest uncertainty is omitted-field breadth. Changing Other's reference weight from 40 to **30 or 55**, while retaining the same method, gives Other approximately **36.23% or 51.01%**. Changing sequencing's multiplier from 1.65 to **1.30 or 2.00** gives sequencing approximately **13.99% or 18.92%**. These are sensitivity scenarios, not statistical confidence intervals. They show why I am more confident in the broad ranking than in small differences between neighboring options.

I prioritized official Nobel records, award-body records, institutional accounts and primary scientific work. I excluded unverifiable claims from an auxiliary comparison and did not use market prices in the numerical estimate. Published prize recipients are not independent observations of Nobel intent, citation recognition is not an annual conversion rate, and absence of a recent prize is not proof of absence from Nobel deliberations.

One concrete source-quality issue is the Gairdner 2026 page: its heading and publication date say **31 March 2026**, but a body dateline says 2025. The 2026 award identities and later official material agree, so I treat that as an apparent dateline error rather than reclassifying the awards. I also distinguish award cycles from announcements and ceremonies throughout. ([gairdner.org](https://www.gairdner.org/resource-hub/2026-canada-gairdner-award-winners))

**Bottom line:** sequencing-by-synthesis is the clearest listed leader, but there is no public evidence of a decisive Nobel shortlist position. Multiple independently recognized omitted discoveries justify a larger combined probability for Other than for any single named option.

## Forecast summary

**As of October 2, 2026 at 14:05 UTC, sequencing-by-synthesis is my leading named discovery, with probability 0.152807. Other is the largest overall category, at 0.308331, because it combines numerous plausible discoveries omitted from the twelve-item list.** No individual discovery is sufficiently dominant to justify a high-confidence prediction.

The most consequential recent evidence is the **2026 Wolf Prize in Chemistry for David Klenerman, Shankar Balasubramanian and Pascal Mayer**, recognizing large-scale, inexpensive DNA sequencing. This directly strengthens the sequencing-by-synthesis option. Conversely, all three discovery groups in Clarivate’s **2026 Chemistry** selections fall outside the supplied options. Those two findings substantially influence the forecast, but neither reveals the Nobel committee’s decision. ([wolffund.org.il](https://wolffund.org.il/david-klenerman/?utm_source=openai))

## 1. Resolution, timing and information cutoff

The official schedule places the Chemistry announcement on **Wednesday, October 7, 2026, at 11:45 CEST at the earliest**, equivalent to 09:45 UTC. That is approximately **4 days, 19 hours and 40 minutes** after the forecast cutoff. I am forecasting the forthcoming official motivation, not attempting to resolve the question using an earlier scientific prize. Earlier discoveries and awards are evidence about the future Nobel decision. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/about/prize-announcement-dates/?sm_guid=Mjk3MzM1fDI0MDExMjE4fC0xfHJzaGFsZXR0QHJlc2VhcmNoYW1lcmljYS5vcmd8MjM3MTYzMXx8MHwwfDI5NzY0NzA3MXw5NTN8MHwwfHwyNjI2NDR8MA2&utm_source=openai))

I apply the supplied discovery-based resolution rules literally:

- A different laureate lineup does not invalidate an otherwise matching discovery.
- A prize for PHOLEDs or another efficient OLED approach could match the OLED option even if Tang or Van Slyke were not laureates.
- A prize for base editing, protein electron transfer or proteomics would be Other, despite connections to DNA or proteins.
- If two discoveries receive equal shares, the first discovery in the announcement determines resolution; otherwise the larger share determines resolution.

The remaining uncertainty is primarily about a confidential institutional choice, not whether scientists will make a new breakthrough during the next five days. NobelPrize.org describes recommendations being submitted in September and the Academy selecting laureates in early October. Nomination and evaluation material remains confidential for 50 years. I therefore do not treat public contender lists as an official shortlist or assume that late publicity can change an already advanced selection process. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/chemistry?utm_source=openai))

## 2. Research approach and decision-relevant findings

I investigated four questions that could materially change the forecast: **whether there was fresh, discovery-specific award recognition; whether the listed options omitted credible contenders; whether recent recognition belonged to Chemistry rather than Physics or Medicine; and whether newer technologies had reached convincing practical maturity.** I used official Nobel records, the Nobel-data API through the available data tools, prize foundations, institutional announcements and original research records. I also commissioned separate research into omitted-topic risk and the comparative readiness of sequencing, DNA synthesis, OLEDs and chaperones, plus an independently checked Wolf-to-Nobel historical table.

I did not use prediction-market prices, betting odds or public numerical forecast aggregates. The scoring and normalization below are independent judgments based on non-market evidence.

### A. Fresh recognition materially strengthens sequencing-by-synthesis

The Wolf Foundation identifies Klenerman, Balasubramanian and Mayer as its **2026 Chemistry** laureates. Its description of Mayer’s contribution explicitly connects surface-based DNA-colony amplification with Solexa’s sequencing-by-synthesis chemistry. This makes the match more precise than a generic award for genomics. Contemporaneous Israeli reporting dated **October 1, 2026** establishes that the announcement preceded the client’s question; I do not depend on an October 2 institutional article with an unspecified publication time to establish availability before the cutoff. ([wolffund.org.il](https://wolffund.org.il/david-klenerman/?utm_source=openai))

Two additional 2026 recognitions support the same discovery: the Princess of Asturias jury announced the trio on **May 13, 2026**, and the University of Zurich announced their Gretener-Thürlemann Prize on **August 27, 2026**, explicitly in Chemistry. Zurich describes the surface immobilization, fluorescent nucleotide incorporation, successive removal of the fluorescent label and parallel reading of DNA fragments. It also emphasizes that this is an integrated parallel-sequencing platform, rather than simply one new chemical reaction. ([fpa.es](https://www.fpa.es/en/princess-of-asturias-awards/laureates/2026-david-klenerman-shankar-balasubramanian-pascal-mayer/?texto=acta&utm_source=openai))

**Forecast effect:** I give the combined fresh recognition a substantial but bounded uplift. In the numerical model, sequencing’s underlying weight rises from 11.0 to 17.6, a **1.6-fold relative-weight multiplier**. This multiplier is my judgment, not an estimated empirical likelihood ratio. Holding the other final inputs fixed, it increases sequencing’s blended probability from **0.103189 to 0.152807**. I apply one combined uplift rather than multiplying the three awards separately, because they are correlated recognitions of the same scientific achievement.

### B. Other contains identifiable competitors, not just an unspecified surprise

Clarivate’s release, published **September 17, 2026 at 03:05 ET**, recognizes three Chemistry discovery groups absent from the slate:

1. **Self-assembled monolayers:** David Allara, Ralph Nuzzo and Jacob Sagiv.
2. **Long-range electron transfer in proteins:** Harry Gray and Jay Winkler.
3. **Base editing and prime editing:** David Liu.

These are distinct from controlled radical polymerization, chaperones, sequencing, phosphoramidite synthesis and nanoparticle delivery. Clarivate explicitly states that its program does not aim to predict Nobel recipients in a particular year. I use these selections as evidence of omitted Nobel-caliber work, not as three equally likely finalists. ([ir.clarivate.com](https://ir.clarivate.com/news-events/press-releases/news-details/2026/Clarivate-Reveals-Citation-Laureates-2026-Recognizing-Transformative-Scientific-Breakthroughs/default.aspx?utm_source=openai))

A further omitted discovery is **modern systems proteomics**, recognized in the 2026 Canada Gairdner awards through John Yates, Ruedi Aebersold and Matthias Mann. The same announcement also recognizes Jeffery Kelly’s work on pathological protein aggregation. Neither systems proteomics nor a motivation centered on chemically stabilizing aggregation-prone proteins would automatically match the chaperone option. ([gairdner.org](https://www.gairdner.org/resource-hub/2026-canada-gairdner-award-winners))

There is counter-evidence against an excessively large Other allocation: **metal–organic frameworks were already awarded the Chemistry Nobel on October 8, 2025**, removing a major previously unrecognized materials topic from the realistic near-term omitted pool. This does not eliminate unrelated materials discoveries, but it reduces the attractiveness of immediately rewarding a very closely adjacent framework discovery. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2025/press-release/?gsid=bbb66e8a-80d7-4f9d-9342-c8507afd9b83&utm_source=openai))

**Forecast effect:** I retain roughly 31% for Other. It represents several substantial alternatives plus a long tail, not a claim that any single omitted discovery outranks sequencing.

### C. Category assignment limits the implications of OLED and chaperone recognition

Clarivate’s September 2026 recognition of Adachi, Forrest and Thompson for high-efficiency PHOLED/TADF work is under **Physics**, not Chemistry. This supports OLEDs’ scientific stature but is not a direct Chemistry-specific signal. I do not penalize the option merely because its listed names differ; the relevant issue is the discovery’s potential Nobel category. ([ir.clarivate.com](https://ir.clarivate.com/news-events/press-releases/news-details/2026/Clarivate-Reveals-Citation-Laureates-2026-Recognizing-Transformative-Scientific-Breakthroughs/default.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Chaperones likewise have strong recognition, but much of it is framed as life science or medicine. Hartl and Horwich received the **2011 Lasker Basic Medical Research Award** for chaperone-assisted folding, while Keio announced Hartl as a **2026 Medical Science Prize** recipient on **September 18, 2026**. These make chaperones credible Nobel candidates, while leaving open whether Chemistry is their most likely destination. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/chaperone-assisted-protein-folding/))

**Forecast effect:** Both discoveries receive meaningful probabilities, but less than their generic scientific importance alone might suggest. This is an unconditional Chemistry forecast made before the October 5 Medicine and October 6 Physics announcements; I do not assume either forthcoming result.

### D. Targeted degradation has crossed an important practical threshold

The FDA approved **vepdegestrant on May 1, 2026**, describing it as a heterobifunctional protein degrader. This is concrete therapeutic validation relevant to the targeted-protein-degradation option. I therefore do not rely on the outdated argument that this technology has no approved therapeutic implementation. Nevertheless, one recent approval is not equivalent to the decades of broad use behind sequencing, polymerization or OLEDs. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/resources-information-approved-drugs/fda-approves-vepdegestrant-er-positive-her2-negative-esr1-mutated-advanced-or-metastatic-breast))

The 2004 Chemistry Nobel recognized ubiquitin-mediated degradation itself. The listed option concerns the distinct chemical strategy of redirecting ubiquitin ligases with small molecules. The earlier prize is therefore contextual overlap, not automatic disqualification. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/lists/all-nobel-prizes-in-chemistry/all/?gallery_style=page&utm_source=openai))

## 3. Historical base rates and their limitations

| B: biological chemistry and biological tools | 2002, 2003, 2004, 2006, 2008, 2009, 2012, 2014, 2015, 2017, 2018, 2020, 2024 | 13 | 0.500000 |
| S: synthesis and catalysis | 2001, 2005, 2010, 2021, 2022 | 5 | 0.192308 |
| M: materials and supramolecular chemistry | 2000, 2011, 2016, 2019, 2023, 2025 | 6 | 0.230769 |
| P: physical/theoretical chemistry | 2007, 2013 | 2 | 0.076923 |

The motivations are official; these four classifications are my analytical choices, not Nobel Foundation categories. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/lists/all-nobel-prizes-in-chemistry/all/?gallery_style=page&utm_source=openai))

This history prevents an overly narrow interpretation of Chemistry and provides a constraint on the candidate-based assessment. It does **not** establish that a field is due because it has waited a long time, or that adjacent fields cannot win consecutively. I give the historical-family model only 35% of the final ensemble weight because the bins are debatable and the sample is small.

### Wolf recognition is meaningful, but far from decisive

The independently checked historical table contains **17 Wolf Chemistry award periods covering 2001–2025**. The periods are 2001, 2004, 2005, 2006/7, 2008/9, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2025. Combined labels 2006/7 and 2008/9 are counted once each. Only **two periods** included a same-year Chemistry Nobel winner: **2001**, with Noyori and Sharpless, and **2022**, with Bertozzi. The descriptive frequency is **2/17 = 0.117647**. The comparison joins Wolf’s historical laureate records to official Nobel records, excluding the unannounced 2026 Nobel. ([wolffund.org.il](https://wolffund.org.il/category/field/chemistry/?utm_source=openai))

This is an award-period overlap rate, not an individual scientist’s probability and not sequencing’s forecast probability. The positive matches were verified as pre-Nobel announcements; exact original announcement dates were not independently established for every negative cohort. Furthermore, the 2026 Wolf announcement is unusually close to Nobel week. These limitations make the historical result useful mainly as a warning against treating a Wolf award as a near-certain immediate Nobel signal.

## 5. Numerical model and exact reproduction

I combine two models: a **candidate-specific model**, which responds directly to the evidence, and a **historical-family model**, which limits excessive concentration in any field.

### Model A: candidate-specific normalization

The final inputs are:

| Discovery | Family | Weight w |
|---|---|---:|
| Controlled radical polymerization | S | 9.0 |
| Sequencing-by-synthesis | B | 17.6 |
| Perovskite solar cells | M | 3.5 |
| Phosphoramidite DNA synthesis | B | 7.0 |
| C–H functionalization | S | 7.5 |
| Nanoparticle delivery | B | 6.5 |
| Targeted protein degradation | B | 5.0 |
| Molecular chaperones | B | 5.5 |
| Nanopore sequencing | B | 4.0 |
| Ab initio molecular dynamics | P | 3.5 |
| Efficient OLEDs | M | 6.0 |
| DNA origami | M | 2.5 |
| Other | Across families | 32.0 |

The weights sum to **109.6**. For each outcome, **A(i) = w(i) / 109.6**. Other’s weight represents the combined omitted pool, not one discovery of extraordinary strength.

### Model B: historical-family allocation

Use the historical family probabilities **13/26, 5/26, 6/26 and 2/26**. Within each family, retain the named weights above and add an omitted-discovery reserve:

| Family | Historical probability | Named weights summed | Omitted reserve o | Denominator D |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| B | 13/26 | 45.6 | 18.0 | 63.6 |
| S | 5/26 | 16.5 | 6.0 | 22.5 |
| M | 6/26 | 12.0 | 10.0 | 22.0 |
| P | 2/26 | 3.5 | 4.0 | 7.5 |

For a named discovery i in family g, **B(i) = historical_probability(g) × w(i) / D(g)**. For Other, **B(Other) = Σ historical_probability(g) × o(g) / D(g)**. The within-family reserves are subjective judgments about omitted competition and need not sum to Model A’s aggregate reserve.

### Final ensemble

The final probability is **P(i) = 0.65 × A(i) + 0.35 × B(i)**. The 65/35 split favors discovery-specific evidence while retaining a meaningful historical constraint; it is not a fitted or backtested coefficient.

For example:

- Sequencing: **A = 0.160583942**, **B = 0.138364780**, giving **P = 0.152807235**.
- Other: **A = 0.291970803**, **B = 0.338712231**, giving **P = 0.308330303**.

I calculated the complete distribution in Python. The returned probabilities are rounded to six decimal places, with the rounding residual assigned to Other so that they sum exactly to **1.000000**.

## 6. Robustness, evidence quality and uncertainty

I stress-tested eight combinations of three assumptions: sequencing’s recognition multiplier at **1.2 or 2.1** rather than 1.6; all omitted reserves at **75% or 125%** of their central values; and Model A’s ensemble share at **45% or 85%** rather than 65%. Keeping the remaining inputs fixed gives sequencing probabilities from **0.109459 to 0.210152**, and Other probabilities from **0.230970 to 0.378842**. These are model-sensitivity ranges, not statistical confidence intervals or exhaustive bounds.

Important evidence-quality precautions were:

- **Cutoff verification:** the October 1 Wolf reporting establishes pre-question availability even though some institutional pages are dated October 2 without a publication hour.
- **Correlated recognition:** multiple prizes for sequencing do not count as independent committee signals.
- **Category verification:** the 2026 OLED recognition is Physics; it is not mislabeled as a Chemistry selection.
- **Historical sample discipline:** the Nobel sample has 26 annual prizes; the Wolf comparison has 17 award periods, not 25 annual observations.
- **Publication versus discovery dates:** an old institutional recognition is not presented as fresh evidence. The original DNA-origami paper is from 2006; the Merkin announcement is from 2023; the Keio announcement and FDA approval are genuinely from 2026.
- **No automatic maturity requirement:** commercial or clinical use strengthens some cases, but I do not assume it is necessary for a Nobel.
- **No claim of confidential access:** I found no reliable disclosure of the actual 2026 motivation or committee shortlist.

The six decimal places make the calculations auditable; they do **not** imply that the underlying probabilities are known to one-millionth precision. The defensible substantive conclusion is that **sequencing-by-synthesis leads the named discoveries, the remaining named contenders are individually much less likely, and a substantial omitted-discovery reserve remains necessary**.

This forecast uses the client’s information boundary of October 2, 2026, at 14:18 UTC ([forecast inputs](sandbox:/mnt/data/chemistry_forecast_inputs.json)). The Chemistry announcement is scheduled for October 7, 2026, at 11:45 CEST at the earliest, equivalent to 09:45 UTC ([official schedule](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/about/prize-announcement-dates/)). The supplied profiles are the main evidence for comparing named options. I accept their figures as stipulated. ## Evidence
The historical backbone is the supplied comparison group of 61 Chemistry laureates awarded during 2000–2025, measured using their pre-prize records ([reference-class definitions](sandbox:/mnt/data/chemistry_forecast_inputs.json)). These benchmarks give a common scale for impact, translation, and educational reach. They also leave room for different kinds of achievement. The Chemistry prize has recognized theoretical methods, as illustrated by the 1998 award for density-functional theory and computational quantum chemistry ([official award](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1998/summary/)). I therefore do not let patent intensity become a requirement for winning.

Other needs substantial probability because the list omits several independently recognized discovery families. These include self-assembled molecular surface coatings, recognized by the 2022 Kavli Prize; carbon–heteroatom cross-coupling, recognized by the 2019 Wolf Prize; activity-based protein profiling, recognized by the 2022 Wolf Prize; and programmable carbohydrate synthesis, recognized by the 2014 Wolf Prize ([Kavli](https://www.kavliprize.org/prizes/nanoscience/2022), [catalytic coupling](https://wolffund.org.il/category/field/page/7/), [chemical proteomics](https://wolffund.org.il/benjamin-f-cravatt-iii/), [carbohydrate synthesis](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/829549)). Clarivate’s current Chemistry selections add concrete examples outside the list: self-assembled monolayers, long-range electron transfer in proteins, and base/prime editing ([2026 selections](https://clarivate.com/citation-laureates/chemistry/)). These establish omitted scope, not the Nobel Committee’s shortlist.

I assign Other 38.0%, leaving 62.0% for named discoveries ([coverage judgment and calculation](sandbox:/mnt/data/chemistry_forecast_inputs.json)). This is a judgment about prospective coverage, not a historical hit rate. The named discoveries span several strong scientific traditions, but adjacent sequencing, nucleic-acid, and chemical-biology entries do not independently guarantee comprehensive coverage.

For the named options, I separate career strength from evidence tied to the discovery. The career score assigns 45% weight to the three scholarly-impact comparisons, 35% to invention and patent comparisons, and 20% to book-reach comparisons. At option level, it combines the mean of the strongest two researchers, the mean of all named researchers, and the strongest researcher, with weights of 60%, 20%, and 20%. This prevents a weaker third publication record from becoming a veto when the actual laureates need not match the proposed trio ([scoring inputs](sandbox:/mnt/data/chemistry_forecast_inputs.json)).

The discovery score uses one relevant anchor paper per option. Its weights are 10% impact, 15% disruption, 25% foundation share, 40% invention citations, and 10% book citations. Counts are log-scaled, and unavailable disruption or foundation values receive a neutral midpoint. All attributes come from the same paper; I do not manufacture an exceptional paper by combining different papers’ best features. Shared papers and invention counts are not added repeatedly ([anchor papers and transformations](sandbox:/mnt/data/chemistry_forecast_inputs.json)).

I average career-centered, balanced, and discovery-centered cases. Their career fractions are 0.80, 0.50, and 0.25, with mixture weights of 0.20, 0.50, and 0.30. Within each case, conditional probabilities are proportional to \(\exp(5S_i)\), where \(S_i\) is the combined profile score. These are judgmental weights, not fitted selection coefficients. Publication volume and collaboration counts receive no separate bonus, avoiding another reward for breadth already represented elsewhere ([complete calculation](sandbox:/mnt/data/chemistry_forecast_inputs.json)).

After normalization, these changes move about 2% of conditional named-option probability mass, leaving the ranking principally profile-driven ([adjustment calculation](sandbox:/mnt/data/chemistry_forecast_inputs.json)). ## What's non-obvious
Discovery matching matters more than matching famous names. Hartwig winning for carbon–heteroatom coupling would not automatically make C–H functionalization correct; the independently recognized coupling contribution has a different chemical core ([Wolf citation](https://wolffund.org.il/category/field/page/7/)). The same distinction prevents Schreiber’s broad chemical-biology record or Langer’s entire biomaterials career from becoming direct evidence for every discovery associated with them ([profile treatment](sandbox:/mnt/data/chemistry_forecast_inputs.json)).

The OLED recognition signal also needs careful reading. Clarivate places its current advanced-OLED selection under Physics, not Chemistry ([primary announcement](https://ir.clarivate.com/news-events/press-releases/news-details/2026/Clarivate-Reveals-Citation-Laureates-2026-Recognizing-Transformative-Scientific-Breakthroughs/default.aspx)). That does not exclude a Chemistry award, but it is not a Chemistry-specific boost. Likewise, recent prizes and clinical milestones establish recognition or usefulness, not access to the Nobel decision. The official process places recommendations before the Academy’s early-October vote and keeps nominations and evaluations confidential for 50 years ([selection process](https://www.nobelprize.org/chemistry)).

## Uncertainties
The largest gap is the private selection evidence: the actual nominee pool, expert assessments, and committee recommendations. Public profiles cannot reveal those assessments under the confidentiality rules ([Nobel process](https://www.nobelprize.org/chemistry)). The eventual motivation also matters. A broad or divided award could cross discovery boundaries, making the client’s share and ordering rules decisive ([resolution terms](sandbox:/mnt/data/chemistry_forecast_inputs.json)).

The main numerical uncertainties are shortlist coverage and how strongly to distinguish good profiles. Stress tests varying Other from 28% to 48% and the score-concentration coefficient from four to six put OLEDs at roughly 7–12%, delivery at 5–8%, and perovskites at 6–9% ([sensitivity calculation](sandbox:/mnt/data/chemistry_forecast_inputs.json)). These are model-sensitivity ranges, not statistical confidence intervals. Comparable profiles for omitted discoveries and historical nominee-versus-winner records would sharpen the coverage and weighting judgments. The six-decimal probability fields preserve the calculation and exact normalization; they do not claim six-decimal knowledge of the committee’s choice.

## Forecast basis and cutoff

The Nobel process offers almost no legitimate candidate-specific information: nominations, expert reports, opinions and dissents remain confidential for 50 years. The published timetable says expert assessment occurs in March–May, the committee writes its report in June–August, the Chemistry Section discusses it in September, and the Academy makes the final decision by majority vote in early October. Thus, current awards and publicity can be weak corroborating signals, but they are not evidence of the confidential decision. 

I did **not** consult prediction-market prices, betting odds or forecast aggregates.

## Quantitative procedure

### 1. Probability assigned to Other

I assigned **0.430** to Other before dividing probability among the named discoveries. This is high because the scientific outcome space is much broader than the twelve named options. For example, Clarivate's 2026 Chemistry selections concern self-assembled monolayers, long-range electron transfer in proteins, and base/prime editing—none of which matches a named option. Chemistry World's own 2026 discussion also included an explicit pick for skeletal editing, another Other outcome. These are not reliable Nobel indicators, but they demonstrate that substantial omitted-candidate mass remains. ([japanprize.jp](https://www.japanprize.jp/en/press_kits2024.html?utm_source=openai))

Conversely, the supplied list includes many of the most persistent Nobel-scale candidates in synthesis, polymers, computational chemistry, sequencing, chemical biology and materials science. I therefore put aggregate named-option coverage above 50%, at **0.570**, rather than making Other overwhelmingly dominant.

### 2. Profile-only score

I treated the supplied profiles as true and made them the primary comparative evidence. For each person I computed:

`person score = 0.15(median-impact comparison) + 0.15(top-10%-work comparison) + 0.15(top-1%-work comparison) + 0.20(citing-inventions comparison) + 0.15(own-patents comparison) + 0.10(works-cited-by-books comparison) + 0.10(distinct-citing-books comparison)`

All comparisons were converted to 0–1 values; “higher than all” was entered as 1 and “lower than all” as 0.

Because resolution is by discovery and the named people need not exactly equal the eventual laureates, I did not let a weak third profile dominate an option. The option-level score was:

`option profile score = 0.60(mean of two strongest person scores) + 0.20(mean of all named person scores) + 0.20(strongest person score)`

I converted these scores into baseline named-option probabilities proportional to:

`exp[3 × (option profile score − 0.65)]`

and scaled them to total 0.570.

## 1. Evidence hierarchy and coverage

The **client-supplied profiles are the principal evidence for the relative probabilities of all twelve named options**. I take their figures as given, without auditing author attribution or discounting the records for their publication cutoff.

The profile evidence comprises **34 named researchers**, grouped into twelve discovery options. Publication windows differ by researcher, as specified in the profiles. I do not pool those windows into a single exposure-adjusted citation rate or sum overlapping coauthors' publications.

The reference comparisons concern **61 Chemistry laureates awarded during 2000–2025**, measured using their pre-prize records. A statement that a researcher exceeds 92% of those laureates is used as a comparative score of 0.92—not as a 92% probability of winning. The supplied work-impact and disruption percentiles are likewise used on their stated 0–1 scales. Foundation shares are proportions; invention, patent, book, and collaborator measures are counts.

External information serves two narrower purposes: assessing how much probability belongs to **Other**, and making a small secondary adjustment for a verified recent award. I did not consult prediction-market prices, betting odds, or public forecast aggregates.

The institutional evidence argues against excessive concentration. The Academy describes an expert evaluation process culminating in an Academy decision, not an automatic bibliometric selection rule.  Nominations, discussions, and evaluations remain confidential for fifty years, so public profiles cannot establish the actual 2026 shortlist. 

## 2. Translating the profiles into comparable scores

I used a transparent scoring model, calculated in Python. Its weights are forecasting judgments, not coefficients estimated from a historical training sample. To reduce dependence on any one judgment about what Nobel committees reward, I averaged three different weighting schemes.

### Researcher-level measures

For each researcher, I calculated four career measures:

- **Impact, I:** the mean of the three supplied past-laureate reference comparisons for median work impact, share of works in the top 10%, and share in the top 1%, after dividing percentages by 100.
- **Technological translation, T:** 0.60 times the reference comparison for distinct citing inventions, plus 0.40 times the comparison for own US utility patents.
- **Textbook reach, B:** 0.40 times the reference comparison for works cited by books, plus 0.60 times the comparison for distinct citing books. Distinct books receive slightly more weight because they indicate breadth of transmission.
- **Collaboration, C:** 0.50 × ln(1 + number of distinct Nobel-laureate coauthors)/ln(8), plus 0.50 × ln(1 + people who are both coauthors and co-inventors)/ln(400). The denominators correspond to the largest supplied counts: seven Nobel coauthors and 399 overlapping collaborators.

Collaboration receives only 2% of each final score. It is a weak supporting signal, not a claim that collaboration with laureates causes selection.

For each discovery, each career measure is aggregated as:

**Option measure = 0.65 × highest named researcher's measure + 0.35 × mean of the named researchers' measures.**

This emphasizes a discovery's strongest associated record without ignoring its supporting researchers. It also avoids making a two-person option automatically weaker than a three-person option. This treatment is appropriate because the question does not require the named people to match the actual laureates. The Academy's rules also allow at most three people to share a prize. 

### Discovery-specific defining-work measure

Career strength alone can reward a researcher for accomplishments other than the listed discovery. I therefore calculated a separate **defining-work score, D**, from the discovery-relevant papers in the supplied profiles:

**D = 0.45 × ln(1 + citing inventions)/ln(5090) + 0.20 × disruption percentile + 0.25 × foundation share + 0.10 × impact percentile.**

The invention normalization uses the largest supplied relevant-paper count, 5,089. Logarithms prevent a very large patent-citation count from overwhelming every other measure. For a paper with unavailable disruption or foundation values, I use 0.50 for the missing component. That is a neutral imputation, not an assertion that its unobserved value equals 0.50.

For option i in scheme m, let S(i,m) be its weighted score. I convert scores into a distribution conditional on a named option winning:

**q(i,m) = exp(6 × S(i,m)) / Σj exp(6 × S(j,m)).**

**q(i) = 0.40q(i,balanced) + 0.40q(i,discovery-centered) + 0.20q(i,academic-impact-centered).**

These models use overlapping evidence and are not statistically independent. Averaging them represents uncertainty about the appropriate valuation of that evidence. ## 2. Decision-relevant research threads

### A. Should whole-career strength or discovery-specific evidence dominate?

Whole-career profiles strongly favor drug delivery and, through Schreiber, targeted degradation. However, the question concerns a particular discovery. I therefore give greater aggregate weight to the supplied defining-work evidence while retaining career-wide impact, translation, educational reach, and collaboration as substantial corroboration.

This distinction matters especially for Schreiber’s ferroptosis, chromatin, and calcineurin works; Hartwig’s aryl-halide amination work; Miyasaka’s tin-based storage material; and Tang’s organic photovoltaic cell. Those remain part of their person-level profiles, but I do not use them as defining-work evidence for, respectively, targeted ligase redirection, C–H functionalization, perovskite solar cells, or OLEDs.

### B. Should a weaker third profile reduce the probability of a discovery?

Only modestly. The laureates need not match the proposed trio, so an equal-person average is inappropriate. Conversely, a pure maximum would let one exceptionally broad career dominate an option. My aggregation gives **70% weight to the strongest person-level composite and 30% to the mean of the named profiles**, without summing people or adding a three-person-team bonus.

### C. Can historical prize frequencies calibrate Other directly?

No. I retrieved the **26 annual Chemistry awards from 2000 through 2025** using the Nobel data service and checked official motivations. The history spans materials, catalysis, biological mechanisms, analytical methods, computational chemistry, and energy storage. But this is a curated list of prospective 2026 candidates, not a taxonomy specified before those historical awards. Counting how often these exact current labels appeared historically would not provide a valid prospective hit rate.

The official process also limits certainty: nominations, investigations, and opinions are confidential for **50 years**; recommendations are prepared before the Academy’s early-October selection. Public profile strength does not reveal the committee’s actual shortlist or preferences.

## 3. Reproducible scoring model

The model is a transparent judgmental conversion of the supplied evidence into probabilities. Its weights are not coefficients fitted to a historical selection dataset.

### Step 1: Four person-level features

For person j, convert each supplied ‘higher than x% of the reference laureates’ comparison into r = x/100. ‘Higher than all’ becomes 1 and ‘lower than all’ becomes 0.

Define:

- **I:** mean of the three benchmark features for median impact, share of works in the cohort top 10%, and share in the top 1%.
- **T:** 0.75 × citing-invention benchmark + 0.25 × own-patent benchmark.
- **B:** 0.40 × works-cited-by-books benchmark + 0.60 × distinct-citing-books benchmark.
- **C:** 0.50 × min(number of distinct Nobel laureate co-authors / 3, 1) + 0.50 × min[ln(1 + co-author/co-inventor count) / ln(101), 1].

The collaboration cap prevents large networks from overwhelming the scientific evidence. Collaboration receives only 5% of each career composite and approximately **1.69% of the ensemble’s underlying score weight**.

For scenario m, compute each person’s career score from its I/T/B/C weights. For discovery i, aggregate those scores as:

`Q(i,m) = 0.70 × maximum person score + 0.30 × mean person score`.

### Step 2: Discovery-related defining-work features

I screen the supplied defining works for relevance to the named discovery, admitting directly related precursors, implementations, and reviews but excluding unrelated achievements. For each option, take the maximum available relevant value separately for:

- d: disruption percentile;
- f: foundation share;
- u: reported citing-invention count;
- v: reported citing-book count.

These maxima are an evidence envelope, not a claim that one paper simultaneously attains all four values. Shared papers are not added repeatedly. I also do not sum paper-level invention counts, because the supplied data do not establish their deduplicated union.

## 5. Why Other receives 30%

I estimate Other separately rather than pretending it has a comparable three-person profile. **30% is a judgment about residual discovery coverage**, not an empirical frequency estimated from 26 historical awards.

The official **2025 award for metal–organic frameworks**, announced on 8 October 2025, is itself outside this list. This illustrates the breadth of possible Chemistry motivations, although it does not imply that another framework discovery is likely immediately afterward.

Concrete omitted discovery families include:

- **Carbon–heteroatom cross-coupling**, including Buchwald–Hartwig chemistry. The Wolf Foundation’s 2019 description specifically concerns transition-metal catalysts forming carbon–heteroatom bonds. A motivation centered on that advance would not automatically match C–H functionalization merely because Hartwig were a laureate.
- **Activity-based protein profiling and chemical proteomics.** The Wolf Foundation’s 2022 Cravatt citation documents this distinct discovery family, which is not equivalent to small molecules redirecting ubiquitin ligases.
- **Programmable and chemoenzymatic carbohydrate synthesis.** Scripps describes Wong’s methods for synthesizing oligosaccharides and glycoproteins, another substantial family absent from the named options.

These examples establish genuine residual scope; they are not a complete ranked shortlist. Conversely, the twelve supplied options are a selected collection of strong discoveries, and the profiles supply substantial evidence for them collectively. I therefore reserve **70% for named outcomes**, rather than assigning Other a majority.

I apply no mandatory subfield-rotation rule and no requirement that an award use the exact proposed laureate trio. The historical evidence and official process shape the residual uncertainty, not the principal named-option ranking.

## 6. Sensitivity, limitations, and interpretation

I calculated sensitivity to a score-to-probability coefficient from **4 to 8** and strongest-person aggregation weights from **0.50 to 0.90**, retaining the four-scenario ensemble and Other at 30%. OLEDs ranged from approximately **11.14% to 19.69%**, drug delivery from **8.06% to 9.86%**, and phosphoramidite synthesis from **6.15% to 6.49%**. Allowing Other additionally to range from **20% to 40%** expands the OLED stress range to approximately **9.55%–22.50%**. These are model-sensitivity ranges, not statistically estimated confidence intervals.

The most important uncertainty is the committee’s weighting of exceptional individual discoveries versus broader scientific, technological, and educational influence. The supplied profiles do not reveal its preferences. The scenario ensemble makes that uncertainty explicit rather than hiding it in one weighting scheme.

The short remaining horizon does not justify a highly concentrated forecast: the selection process is already advanced, but its decisive evidence is confidential. My conclusion is therefore **OLEDs as the strongest named discovery under the stipulated profile-based comparison, with substantial probability spread across other named discoveries and a 30% residual for Other**.

## Forecast summary and resolution interpretation

**Forecast as of October 2, 2026, at 14:05 UTC:** Other is the largest individual outcome at **30%**. Among the named discoveries, my leading choices are **efficient organic light-emitting diodes, 11.75322%**; **nanoparticle drug and nucleic-acid delivery, 9.95939%**; and **solid-state perovskite solar cells, 8.52619%**.

## 1. Evidence hierarchy and data framing

Following the stipulated assumption, **the supplied profiles are the principal evidence for comparing named options**. I accepted their figures and attribution as given. I did not reduce their weight because the publication record ends in 2021 or because the underlying records cannot be independently audited here.

The principal dataset comprises **34 named-person profiles**, compared with the supplied reference group of **61 Chemistry laureates from 2000–2025**. Its stated vintages are the **OpenAlex January 2026 snapshot**, **PatentsView December 31, 2025**, and Reliance on Science patent-to-paper citations. Candidate works and patent grants cover the person-specific starting years reported in the profiles through **2021 inclusive**; the reference laureates are measured using their pre-prize records. These are the supplied data definitions, not independently reconstructed datasets.

The quantities have different meanings, which I preserved in the model:

- Impact and disruption percentiles are **0–1 cohort-relative measures**, using the stated five-year windows.
- Foundation share is a **0–1 proportion**, also measured over five years.
- Citing inventions, own US utility patents, works cited by books, and distinct citing books are **counts**, not annual rates.
- The reference lines report the percentage of the 61 laureates whose corresponding value is below the candidate's value.
- Research-work counts describe the amount of evidence available. I did not independently reward publication volume, which would otherwise count productivity again through several correlated measures.

I used outside evidence only for the breadth of Other, institutional context, and modest adjustments for independently awarded recognition. I also obtained the 2016–2025 Chemistry prize record through the Nobel data provider and commissioned a focused research pass on discoveries outside the choices. **No prediction-market prices, betting odds, or public forecast aggregates were used.**

## 2. Decision-relevant research threads

### A. Does a strong career profile support this particular discovery?

This matters because the outcome is discovery-specific. For example, Hartwig's aryl-halide amination work is not itself evidence of a C–H functionalization breakthrough, and Schreiber's GPX4, chromatin, and calcineurin papers are not themselves the listed targeted-degradation discovery.

I therefore separated **career-level evidence** from **directly relevant defining-work evidence**. Broad career achievements remain in the career scores, while the breakthrough score uses only supplied works relevant to the option. This prevents a highly distinguished scientist's unrelated work from determining the discovery ranking.

### B. Is Other a substantial pool or a thin residual?

The recent official record spans molecular machines, biomolecular structural methods, enzyme engineering, batteries, genome editing, synthetic catalysis, nanomaterials, protein computation, and coordination materials. It does not establish a mechanical disciplinary rotation or an empirical shortlist-hit rate. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/lists/all-nobel-prizes-in-chemistry/2019-2010/?gallery_style=page&utm_source=openai))

The strongest recent adjustment was for sequencing-by-synthesis: the Wolf Foundation identifies Klenerman, Balasubramanian, and Mayer as its **2026 Chemistry laureates** for large-scale DNA sequencing, and dates its 2026 announcement item **September 30, 2026**, before this forecast. ## 3. Reproducible scoring model

The following is a transparent judgmental model, calculated in Python. Its coefficients express how I weigh the supplied evidence; they are not coefficients fitted to a historical Nobel-selection regression.

### Person-level career scores

Convert each reported reference-line percentage to a fraction. For example, higher than 70% becomes 0.70; higher than all becomes 1; lower than all becomes 0. Let r denote these fractions.

For each person:

- **Impact, I:** `0.30*r_median_impact + 0.30*r_top10_share + 0.40*r_top1_share`.
- **Technological translation, T:** `0.65*r_citing_inventions + 0.35*r_own_patents`.
- **Textbook reach, B:** `0.40*r_works_cited_by_books + 0.60*r_distinct_citing_books`.
- **Collaboration, C:** `0.50*ln(1+n_Nobel_coauthors)/ln(8) + 0.50*ln(1+n_coauthor_coinventors)/ln(400)`.

The collaboration counts are distinct people, not summed shared-paper counts. The normalizers correspond to the largest supplied counts: seven Nobel co-authors and 399 people on both sides. Collaboration receives only a small final weight; it is supporting evidence rather than a requirement.

For each discovery, aggregate each career dimension across its named people as:

`discovery_dimension = 0.65*maximum_person_value + 0.35*mean_person_value`.

This emphasizes a standout contributor while retaining evidence of breadth. It does not require every named person to have an equally strong record, and it does not automatically favor three-person options over two-person options.

### Discovery-specific defining-work score

For each relevant supplied work, calculate:

`D_work = 0.20*impact_percentile + 0.25*disruption_percentile + 0.25*foundation_share + 0.20*ln(1+citing_inventions)/ln(5090) + 0.10*ln(1+citing_books)/ln(16)`.

The count normalizers use the largest relevant supplied work-level counts: **5,089 citing inventions** and **15 citing books**. Logarithms allow differences in translation and textbook reach to matter without letting a several-thousand-patent paper overwhelm every other dimension. For reported n/a disruption or foundation values, I use **0.50**, a neutral midpoint—not zero.

For each discovery, D is the maximum score among directly relevant supplied defining works. A shared paper appearing in multiple profiles is not added repeatedly. The selected works are:

| Controlled radical polymerization | Matyjaszewski's atom-transfer controlled/living radical polymerization paper, 1995 |
